description: Exchange the values of two independent local integer variables without a third temporary variable, then return their final values as [first,second]. Perform the exchange using arithmetic or bit operations on those two variables; do not merely construct the reversed result directly.
constraints: Both arguments may be any signed 32-bit integer. The variables are independent value arguments, even when their values are equal; aliasing two references to the same storage location is not part of this callable.

Do not use a temporary swap variable, tuple/destructuring swap, swap helper, or a preconstructed reversed pair. Allocate the returned two-integer collection only after exchanging the two variables. The callable returns the swapped values instead of printing them; caller value arguments remain unchanged.
why: XOR removes a repeated operand: x xor x is zero and x xor zero is x. The first assignment stores the combined information of both inputs. XORing that combination with the old second recovers the original first, then XORing it with the recovered first recovers the original second. No addition/subtraction overflow is required.
correctness: Let the original values be a and b. After the first assignment, first=a xor b and second=b. The second assignment makes second=(a xor b) xor b=a. The third makes first=(a xor b) xor a=b. XOR associativity and cancellation therefore exchange the two values exactly. This remains valid for equal values and all signed bit patterns because the two variables are distinct locations.
walkthrough: With first=9 and second=4, the assignments produce first=13, then second=9, then first=4. The returned pair is [4,9]. If both values are 7, the intermediate first becomes zero but the following assignments recover [7,7].
time: O(1) fixed-width XOR operations.
space: O(1) auxiliary storage; no swap temporary, plus the two-integer output.
edges: Equal inputs, zeros and negative values.
Both signed endpoints; arithmetic overflow must not break exchange.
related: The public function swaps local Java values and prints them; returning those values makes the same exchange observable in the bank.
title: Number Swapper

python.solutionCode:
def SwapWithoutTemporary(first: int, second: int) -> list[int]:
    first ^= second
    second ^= first
    first ^= second
    return [first, second]

description: Count how often each queried word occurs in a tokenized book, ignoring ASCII letter case. Return one count per query in the original query order, including repeated queries. The book is already split into words; tokenization and punctuation removal are not part of this task.
constraints: book and queries are nonnull arrays of 0..1000 nonnull words. Each word has 1..20 ASCII letters A..Z or a..z. Case is ignored, but spelling must otherwise match exactly; a missing word has count zero.
Preserve both arrays and every word. Preprocess the book once to support the batch of queries rather than rescanning the book for every query. Empty book and empty query list are allowed.
why: Many queries share the same book. Normalize case once per occurrence and accumulate counts in a dictionary, then normalize and look up each query. This pays for reading the book once instead of once per requested word.
correctness: After processing any prefix of book, the dictionary count for each normalized word equals its occurrences in that prefix: inserting a new normalized key starts its count and every later occurrence increments it once. Induction gives exact counts for the entire book. A normalized query identifies precisely its case-insensitive equivalence class; lookup returns that count, or zero when no occurrence created its key. Appending answers in query order preserves repeated queries and their positions.
walkthrough: For book=[Red,blue,RED,green] and queries=[red,BLUE,missing,Red], normalized counts are red:2, blue:1, green:1. The answers are [2,1,0,2]. Red and RED contribute to the same count; the repeated red query does not consume a book occurrence.
time: Expected O(B+Q) character work for B book characters and Q query characters, assuming expected constant dictionary access per bounded-length key. Hash-table collisions can worsen this bound.
space: O(D*L+q) storage for D distinct normalized book words of maximum length L and q returned counts; query normalization uses O(L) temporary storage.
edges: Empty book or query array; all queries absent.
Mixed case, repeated book words and repeated queries.
related: The public preprocessing/query API is combined into one batch callable. Nonempty ASCII tokens avoid unspecified tokenization, Unicode and empty-token behavior.

description: Find an intersection point of two CLOSED line segments in the plane. endpoints contains [startA,endA,startB,endB], with each point represented as [x,y]. Return [x,y] for any point belonging to both segments, or [] when they are disjoint. A segment may have zero length. For an overlap of positive length, any point in the overlap is accepted.
constraints: endpoints has exactly four distinct row objects, each containing two integers in -1000..1000. Equal coordinate values and reversed segment directions are allowed. Preserve the outer array, all row objects and values.

The returned coordinates must be finite numbers within absolute coordinate error 0.000001 of a true common point. Endpoints count as intersections. The input coordinates and collinearity decisions are exact integers; a nearly parallel pair must not be treated as collinear.
why: Use cross products rather than slopes, so vertical segments require no division by zero. For nonparallel directions, the two signed cross-product ratios give the position along each segment; both must lie in [0,1]. Parallel segments can intersect only through collinear overlap, where an endpoint of one segment lies on the other. Checking endpoints also handles point segments.
correctness: For nonzero cross(directionA,directionB), solving the two parametric line equations gives unique parameters t and u. The infinite lines meet inside both closed segments exactly when both parameters are in [0,1]; integer numerator/denominator comparisons establish that fact before computing coordinates. If the cross product is zero, the segments are parallel or degenerate. Any common point then implies either coincident point segments or an overlap containing an endpoint. Testing all four endpoints for exact membership in both segments therefore finds an intersection whenever one exists. If no endpoint passes, the parallel/degenerate segments are disjoint. Readonly inputs are never reordered.
walkthrough: Segments [0,0]→[4,4] and [0,4]→[4,0] have t=u=1/2, so return [2,2]. Segments [0,0]→[4,0] and [2,0]→[6,0] overlap: [2,0], [3,0] and [4,0] are all accepted. A point segment [1,1]→[1,1] intersects a diagonal containing [1,1].
time: O(1) exact integer comparisons and a constant number of real arithmetic operations.
space: O(1) auxiliary state and at most two returned numbers.
edges: Vertical/horizontal crossings, endpoint touches and reversed directions.
Parallel separated segments, collinear overlap and identical segments.
One or two zero-length segments, nearly parallel lines and coordinate limits.
related: The public exercise returns an intersection point or null for two bounded segments, including overlapping collinear segments. Empty/numeric arrays replace Point/null while preserving any common-point freedom.

description: Inspect an n by n tic-tac-toe board and return its winning player: 1 or 2. A win requires a complete nonempty row, complete column, or one of the two full corner-to-corner diagonals occupied by that player. Empty cells are 0. Return 0 when neither player has such a line.
constraints: 0 <= n <= 50. The board is square, nonnull, and contains only 0,1,2. The input promises that at most one player has a winning line, so the result is unambiguous. An empty board has no winner.

Preserve the outer array, every original row and all cell values. This callable inspects winning lines, not move legality, turn counts or whether the game should have stopped earlier. A shorter line inside a larger board is not a win.
why: A winning line can only belong to one of a finite set: n rows, n columns and two full diagonals. For each candidate, take its first cell as the proposed player and verify the remaining cells; an empty first cell immediately disqualifies the line. This covers the generic square-board follow-up without assuming the board is always 3 by 3.
correctness: A candidate is reported only when its first cell is nonzero and every cell in that full line equals it, so every reported player has a genuine winning line. Conversely every allowed winning line appears among the examined rows, columns or two diagonals and therefore will be detected. The at-most-one-winner promise makes early return safe even if that player has several winning lines. If no candidate succeeds, neither player has a win and zero is correct.
walkthrough: For [[1,0,2],[0,1,2],[0,0,1]], no row or column is complete, but the main diagonal contains 1,1,1, so player 1 wins. Three adjacent 1 cells on one row of a 4 by 4 board would not be a complete winning line.
time: O(n^2) time: examine at most 2n+2 lines of length n.
space: O(1) auxiliary space; no board copy or history is needed.
edges: Empty and one-cell boards, all-empty board, full board without a winner.
Both diagonal directions, full columns, and nonwinning partial lines in larger boards.
related: The generic n by n form is established by the author's public implementation; no invented game-history validation is added.

description: Return the number of trailing decimal zero digits in n factorial, without constructing the factorial. A trailing zero means a factor of ten at the end of the integer, not any zero digit inside its representation.
constraints: 0 <= n <= 2147483647. Define 0! as 1, which has zero trailing zeros. Return the exact signed 32-bit count. Preserve inputs.
why: A decimal trailing zero consumes one factor 2 and one factor 5. Factorials supply more twos than fives, so only the number of fives matters. Multiples of 25 contribute a second five, multiples of 125 a third, and so on. Repeatedly dividing n by five counts each contribution without growing a power that might overflow.
correctness: For every exponent k>=1, floor(n/5^k) counts exactly the factors among 1..n supplying at least k copies of five. A factor containing t fives appears in exactly t such counts, so their sum is precisely the total five exponent. Twos are at least as numerous, hence this exponent equals the number of factors of ten. Replacing n by floor(n/5) at each iteration produces these successive quotients. Once it reaches zero, no higher power contributes.
walkthrough: For 25!, multiples 5,10,15,20,25 supply five copies of five, and 25 supplies one extra. The successive quotients are 5,1,0, so the result is 6. Counting multiples of five only would incorrectly return 5.
time: O(log_5(n+1)) integer divisions and additions; zero takes constant time.
space: O(1) auxiliary space; the factorial and powers of five are never stored.
edges: Zero and numbers below five.
Just below, at and above powers of five; the maximum signed input.
related: The public power-multiplication loop can overflow at large inputs; division of the remaining quotient avoids that issue.
title: Factorial Zeros

description: Return the smallest absolute difference between one value from first and one from second. The two chosen occurrences must come from different arrays. Return -1 if either array is empty; otherwise return the exact nonnegative difference, which may exceed a signed 32-bit integer.
constraints: Each nonnull input array contains 0..1000 signed 32-bit integers. Duplicates and equal cross-array values are allowed. Preserve both input arrays and their original order; sort private copies if needed.

C#/Java return a signed 64-bit integer, C++ returns long long, Python returns int and JavaScript returns Number. The largest possible result is 4294967295, exactly representable in each result type. Widen BEFORE subtracting; taking abs after an overflowing 32-bit subtraction is incorrect.
why: Sorted copies expose the closest cross-array neighbors without checking every pair. At current values a and b, moving the larger value can only keep or increase the gap while the smaller stays fixed. Record their difference, then advance the smaller side to seek a closer value.
correctness: Consider current sorted values a<=b. Every not-yet-visited value on the second side is at least b, so none can improve the recorded b-a while a stays fixed. Discarding a is safe. The symmetric argument applies when b<a. Every discarded value has therefore been paired with its best remaining candidate, and any candidates skipped earlier were already bounded by an earlier recorded difference. The least recorded difference is the global minimum. Equal values certify the optimal lower bound zero. Empty input has no cross-array pair and uses the explicit -1 convention.
walkthrough: For first=[10,1,20] and second=[14,5], sort copies to [1,10,20] and [5,14]. Record gaps 4 (1,5), 5 (10,5), 4 (10,14), and 6 (20,14), returning 4. For [-2147483648] and [2147483647], the exact answer is 4294967295 rather than an overflowing signed value.
time: O(n log(n+1)+m log(m+1)) sorting time plus O(n+m) pointer advances.
space: O(n+m) for the two private sorted copies; library sorting workspace is bounded by this storage.
edges: Either input empty, duplicates and a shared value.
Signed endpoints and differences above 2147483647.
related: The author sorted two-pointer task is preserved, with an explicit readonly-input convention and widened result correcting overflow in the public demonstration.

description: Return the larger of two signed 32-bit integers without using comparison operators, conditional branches, conditional expressions, or a max/min/sorting helper. Use their sign bits and arithmetic/bit operations to select the answer. Either copy is valid when the arguments are equal.
constraints: Both inputs may be any signed 32-bit integer, including -2147483648 and 2147483647. The result is one original input. Preserve inputs.
Do not use <,>,<=,>=,==,!=, if/switch, a ternary expression, or a helper that performs the comparison for you. Fixed-width unsigned conversion/masking and sign-bit extraction are allowed.
why: The sign of first-second decides which input is larger only when subtraction cannot overflow. If signs differ, the nonnegative input is larger regardless of the wrapped difference. If signs agree, the difference fits signed range and its sign is reliable. Combine those two choices as zero/one selectors instead of branching.
correctness: Let a and b be bits indicating negative inputs, and d indicate a negative 32-bit difference. When a xor b is one, choose first exactly when a is zero. When their xor is zero, choose first exactly when d is zero; equal inputs may choose first. These two cases are disjoint and exhaustive. The computed selector is therefore zero or one and selects precisely a maximum input. A mask derived from the selector copies the chosen input bits. C++ computes the difference in uint32_t and converts the selected exact signed operand arithmetically, avoiding signed-overflow and implementation-defined unsigned-to-signed conversion.
walkthrough: For first=-2147483648 and second=2147483647, subtraction wraps to the positive bit pattern 1. Its sign alone would select the wrong input. The argument signs differ, so the selector instead chooses the nonnegative second input. For 9 and 4, signs agree and the positive difference correctly chooses 9.
time: O(1) fixed-width arithmetic and bit operations.
space: O(1) auxiliary scalar storage.
edges: Opposite signed endpoints, equal values, zero and negatives.
A subtraction that wraps must not influence the opposite-sign choice.
related: A normal max callable omits this exercise's operation restriction and cannot replace it.
title: Number Max

python.signature: def MaximumWithoutComparison(first: int, second: int) -> int
python.starterCode:
def MaximumWithoutComparison(first: int, second: int) -> int:
    return 0
python.solutionCode:
def MaximumWithoutComparison(first: int, second: int) -> int:
    negative_first = (first >> 31) & 1
    negative_second = (second >> 31) & 1
    negative_difference = ((first - second) & 0xFFFFFFFF) >> 31
    different = negative_first ^ negative_second
    choose_first = different * (negative_first ^ 1) + (different ^ 1) * (negative_difference ^ 1)
    mask = -choose_first
    return (first & mask) | (second & ~mask)

description: Write a signed 32-bit integer in English words. Use title-case number words, single spaces, no punctuation, no hyphens and no word "and". Prefix a negative number with "Negative "; zero is "Zero". The largest scale needed is Billion.
constraints: value is any signed 32-bit integer, including -2147483648. Return a nonempty string with no leading/trailing spaces. Examples of the exact convention: 21 -> "Twenty One", 105 -> "One Hundred Five", 1001 -> "One Thousand One".

Use Thousand, Million and Billion for groups of three decimal digits. Omit zero groups completely; do not insert "Zero" between nonzero groups. Widen before negating the minimum signed value. Preserve the input value.
why: Decimal place values naturally split into groups of three digits. Convert each nonzero group using hundreds, tens and the special names below twenty, then attach the appropriate scale. Process the magnitude in 64-bit or arbitrary-precision storage so the most negative signed input can be made positive safely.
correctness: Repeated division by 1000 decomposes the magnitude uniquely into group values from 0 through 999 and their powers of 1000. Hundreds plus a remainder below 100 spell each group exactly; a remainder below twenty uses its direct name, otherwise a tens word plus an optional ones word spells it. Attaching the scale to each nonzero group and joining groups from most significant to least therefore spells the entire magnitude without zero placeholders. The separate zero case supplies Zero, and prefixing Negative only for a negative original value gives the correct sign and required spacing.
walkthrough: For -1002003, the low-to-high groups are 3,2,1. They spell Three, Two Thousand and One Million. Reverse the group order and join once to get One Million Two Thousand Three, then prefix Negative. The result is "Negative One Million Two Thousand Three".
example: Negative One Million Two Thousand Three
time: O(d+o) time for d decimal digits and o returned characters; at most four groups occur in the signed 32-bit domain.
space: O(o) for group words and the final text, with constant-size name tables; at most four chunk records are needed.
edges: Zero, negatives and the minimum signed input.
Teens, exact hundreds/scales and zero groups between nonzero groups.
related: The public integer-to-English task includes negatives. This bank fixes spacing and widens the magnitude rather than inheriting the public minimum-integer negation overflow.
title: English Int

python.signature: def EnglishInteger(value: int) -> str
python.starterCode:
def EnglishInteger(value: int) -> str:
    return ""
python.solutionCode:
def EnglishInteger(value: int) -> str:
    if value == 0:
        return "Zero"
    small = [
        "Zero",
        "One",
        "Two",
        "Three",
        "Four",
        "Five",
        "Six",
        "Seven",
        "Eight",
        "Nine",
        "Ten",
        "Eleven",
        "Twelve",
        "Thirteen",
        "Fourteen",
        "Fifteen",
        "Sixteen",
        "Seventeen",
        "Eighteen",
        "Nineteen",
    ]
    tens = ["", "", "Twenty", "Thirty", "Forty", "Fifty", "Sixty", "Seventy", "Eighty", "Ninety"]
    scales = ["", "Thousand", "Million", "Billion"]
    magnitude = abs(value)
    groups = []
    scale = 0
    while magnitude:
        chunk = magnitude % 1000
        if chunk:
            words = []
            if chunk >= 100:
                words.extend([small[chunk // 100], "Hundred"])
                chunk %= 100
            if chunk >= 20:
                words.append(tens[chunk // 10])
                chunk %= 10
            if chunk:
                words.append(small[chunk])
            if scale:
                words.append(scales[scale])
            groups.append(" ".join(words))
        magnitude //= 1000
        scale += 1
    return ("Negative " if value < 0 else "") + " ".join(reversed(groups))

description: Compute subtraction, multiplication or integer division using addition as the only arithmetic operation. operation is subtract, multiply or divide, meaning first-second, first*second or first/second respectively. Division truncates toward zero, including negative operands.
constraints: first and second are integers in -10000..10000. operation is exactly subtract, multiply or divide. For divide, second is nonzero. These bounds keep every result in signed 32-bit range and make the repeated-addition baseline runnable.

The solution may use addition, assignment, comparisons, Boolean logic, branches and loops. Constants 0, 1 and -1 are allowed. Do not use subtraction, unary negation of a variable, multiplication, division, remainder, bitwise arithmetic, shifts or helpers that perform those operations (including abs). Increment/decrement by addition is allowed. Preserve caller values.

The reference implements sign reversal by repeatedly adding 1 or -1. Multiplication adds a signed addend a counted number of times; division counts whole divisor magnitudes without exceeding the dividend magnitude.
why: Subtraction is addition of the opposite value. Build that opposite by moving the operand toward zero one unit at a time while accumulating the same movement. Multiplication is repeated addition, and division counts how many whole positive divisor magnitudes fit. Choose the signed addend or quotient step up front so no large product needs a second unit-by-unit sign reversal.
correctness: In sign reversal, current+(-accumulated) remains the original value: each unit added to current is also added to accumulated. Reaching current=0 therefore leaves the exact opposite original operand. Adding that opposite proves subtraction. Multiplication adds the correctly signed first operand exactly abs(second) times, so the result has the required magnitude and sign. Division maintains abs(first)=consumedMagnitude+remaining with remaining nonnegative; each accepted divisor removal adds one correctly signed quotient unit. Termination occurs exactly when another whole divisor would exceed the remainder, proving truncation toward zero. Bounds justify all intermediate sums.
walkthrough: For divide(-7,3), obtain magnitude 7 by adding +1 seven times to -7 and accumulating 7. The divisor magnitude is 3 and its additive opposite is -3. Remainders 7->4->1 permit two removals; a third would be negative. The quotient step is -1 because signs differ, so return -2. For multiply(-4,-3), use addend 4 three times, returning 12.
time: O(abs(first)+abs(second)+1) worst-case time on this bounded integer domain: sign reversal and repeated addition/removal use at most proportional unit/count loops. Division has at most abs(first) iterations.
space: O(1) auxiliary scalar storage; no lookup table or arithmetic helper bypass is used.
edges: Zero dividend/factors, same and opposite signs, divisor magnitudes exceeding the dividend.
Truncation toward zero and admitted positive/negative endpoints.
Division by zero and unsupported operation names are outside the stated input domain.
related: The public task provides minus/multiply/divide via addition. This single-operation callable selects those tasks explicitly and bounds the runnable repeated-addition baseline; it does not silently use forbidden built-in arithmetic.
title: Operations

python.signature: def AdditionOnlyArithmetic(first: int, second: int, operation: str) -> int
python.starterCode:
def AdditionOnlyArithmetic(first: int, second: int, operation: str) -> int:
    return 0
python.solutionCode:
def AdditionOnlyArithmetic(first: int, second: int, operation: str) -> int:
    def opposite(value):
        step = 1 if value < 0 else -1
        result = 0
        while value != 0:
            value += step
            result += step
        return result

    if operation == "subtract":
        return first + opposite(second)
    if operation == "multiply":
        count = opposite(second) if second < 0 else second
        addend = opposite(first) if second < 0 else first
        result = 0
        while count > 0:
            result += addend
            count += -1
        return result
    remaining = opposite(first) if first < 0 else first
    divisor = opposite(second) if second < 0 else second
    remove = opposite(divisor)
    step = 1 if (first < 0) == (second < 0) else -1
    result = 0
    while remaining + remove >= 0:
        remaining += remove
        result += step
    return result

description: Return the earliest year from 1900 through 2000, inclusive, in which the greatest number of the supplied people were alive. Each row is [birthYear,deathYear], and a person counts in both their birth and death years. Rows describe distinct people even if their dates agree.
constraints: There are 0..1000 people; every row has exactly two integers with 1900 <= birthYear <= deathYear <= 2000. Preserve the outer array, row objects, dates and input order.
Resolve all population ties by the earliest year. For no people every year has population zero, so return 1900. A person born and deceased in the same year contributes in that year.
why: A birth increases the population starting in its own year. A death decreases it only in the following year because the death year is included. Recording those changes and taking a prefix sum counts all lifetimes without visiting every person in every year. Scan years in increasing order and update the winner only on a strictly larger population to retain the earliest tie.
correctness: Each person contributes +1 at birth and -1 at death+1. Their contribution to the running sum is consequently one exactly during their inclusive lifetime and zero elsewhere. Summing all contributions yields the exact living population in every scanned year. The running best records the largest population seen and changes its year only when that count increases. Increasing-year order therefore chooses the earliest global maximizer, including 1900 for the all-zero empty case.
walkthrough: For [[1900,1901],[1901,1902],[1902,1902]], populations in 1900,1901,1902 are 1,2,2. The first person still counts in 1901 and the third counts in 1902. The maximum is tied, so return 1901 rather than the last tied year.
time: O(p+Y) time for p people and Y=101 admitted years, hence O(p+1) for this fixed domain.
space: O(Y) change counters including a death-after-2000 sentinel; Y is fixed at 101.
edges: No people, same-year lifetimes, duplicate date rows.
Birth coinciding with another death; earliest tied year and the 2000 endpoint.
related: Date rows replace the public Person wrapper; inclusive lifetime and earliest-tie behavior match its delta implementation.
title: Living People

python.signature: def MostPopulatedYear(people: list[list[int]]) -> int
python.starterCode:
def MostPopulatedYear(people: list[list[int]]) -> int:
    return 0
python.solutionCode:
def MostPopulatedYear(people: list[list[int]]) -> int:
    changes = [0] * 102
    for birth, death in people:
        changes[birth - 1900] += 1
        changes[death - 1900 + 1] -= 1
    alive = 0
    best = 0
    answer = 1900
    for offset in range(101):
        alive += changes[offset]
        if alive > best:
            best = alive
            answer = 1900 + offset
    return answer

description: Return every distinct total length obtainable by placing exactly planks wooden planks end to end. Each plank independently has length shorter or longer, with unlimited availability of each kind. Arrangement order does not make a new length. Return the lengths in strictly increasing order.
constraints: 0 <= planks <= 10000 and 1 <= shorter <= longer <= 100000. The largest total is at most 1000000000 and fits signed 32-bit range. Inputs are preserved.
For zero planks return [0], the length of the empty board. When the two lengths agree, return one length, not repeated copies. Return a concrete integer array/list/vector.
why: Only the number of long planks affects the total; the ordering of those planks does not. For k long planks, total length is planks*shorter+k*(longer-shorter). Enumerating k from zero through planks covers all choices without exploring 2^planks arrangements. Equal plank lengths collapse all counts to one answer.
correctness: Every board uses a unique count k of long planks between zero and planks, so its total has the stated formula. Conversely every such k is feasible by choosing k long planks and the rest short. When longer>shorter, increasing k strictly increases the total, proving the generated list is sorted and contains no duplicates. When lengths agree, all choices yield the single emitted total. The k=0 empty-board case yields zero.

space: O(1) auxiliary space excluding the returned O(planks+1) integer values, or one value for equal lengths.
edges: Zero planks, equal lengths, one plank.
Maximum count and lengths, without integer overflow or duplicate totals.

description: Encode an already parsed XML element tree using supplied positive tag/attribute codes. Return an array of string tokens. For each element emit: its decimal name code; each attribute as decimal name code then literal value; "0" ending the attribute list; its nonempty text OR its recursively encoded children in order; and "0" ending the element. If n>0, element 0 is the root; children lists form one rooted tree reaching every element exactly once, with valid node indices and specified sibling order. Nonempty elementTexts is allowed only at a leaf. Empty text means no text token; an empty leaf therefore emits its code followed by two end markers. n=0 encodes to [].

attributeOwners, attributeNames and attributeValues have equal length a in 0..1000. Each owner is a valid element index. Emit attributes of an element in their original attribute-array order, even when attributes of different elements are interleaved. An element has no repeated attribute name.

codeNames and codes have equal length 1..9. codeNames are unique ASCII-letter names of length 1..20; codes are distinct integers 1..9. Every element/attribute name appears in this map. Texts and attribute values contain 0..100 ASCII letters/spaces. This literal domain excludes the reserved digit marker; XML parsing, entities, namespaces and mixed text/child content are outside this already-parsed input model.

All arrays, child row objects, values and order are readonly. Return actual literal tokens, not a whitespace-split string: one attribute value containing spaces remains one token. Numeric code tokens use ordinary decimal spelling, and end markers are exactly "0".
why: XML nesting needs a closing marker after all children, so an ordinary preorder list alone is insufficient. Use explicit enter/exit events: entering emits the code, attributes and first marker; exiting emits the final marker. Put child enter events on the stack in reverse sibling order so they execute in the original order. Group attribute indices by owner once to avoid rescanning every attribute at every element.
correctness: On entry, the name code and every owned attribute pair are emitted in the required order, followed by exactly one attribute terminator. For a text leaf the literal text is emitted before its scheduled exit. Otherwise reverse pushing causes each child subtree to complete in sibling order before the parent exit is processed. By induction on a subtree, these events emit exactly its prescribed encoding and one final marker. The root event therefore emits the whole tree, and empty input emits no events. Attribute buckets preserve original per-owner order and never duplicate a pair. Inputs are only read.
walkthrough: Let element names be [family,person], texts ["",Hello] and children [[1],[]]. Attributes are owners [0,1], names [last,first], values [Tran,Ada]; name codes are family=1, person=2, first=3, last=4. The tokens are ["1","4","Tran","0","2","3","Ada","0","Hello","0","0"]. The last two zeros close person then family; the earlier zeros end their attribute lists.
time: Expected O(n+a+k+T) time for n elements, a attributes, k code mappings and T returned token characters; each event/attribute is visited once and bounded name lookups are hashed.
space: O(n+a+k) auxiliary buckets, event stack and map, plus O(n+a+T) returned token storage. The explicit stack avoids a language call-stack limit on a 1000-element chain.
edges: No elements, empty leaves and text-only leaves.
Interleaved owners, empty/space-containing attribute values, arbitrary code-map order.
Wide sibling groups and 1000-level nested trees with no recursive call overflow.
related: The public XML task encodes an already parsed Element hierarchy with name codes and two kinds of end marker. Parallel arrays are its explicit tree/attribute input representation here; returned string tokens preserve literal boundaries without adding a separate XML-parser exercise.

description: Find a line that divides each of two axis-aligned squares into equal areas. Each row is [left,bottom,side], describing the closed square [left,left+side]×[bottom,bottom+side]. Return [startX,startY,endX,endY], the two outermost boundary intersections of that line across both squares. Either endpoint order is accepted. If the centers coincide, any line through the common center is accepted, with its full outer boundary span.
constraints: squares has exactly two distinct row objects. left and bottom are integers in -1000..1000 and side is an integer in 1..1000. Squares may overlap, touch, contain one another or be identical. Preserve all input objects, rows and values.

Return four finite coordinates. Each endpoint must be within absolute coordinate error 0.000001 of the true outermost endpoint for the chosen bisecting line. The endpoints must be distinct and include the complete intersection span across both squares, including any gap between disjoint squares.
why: Every line through a square center bisects its area by central symmetry. Distinct centers therefore determine the required line. Choose its direction and extend from each center until the larger coordinate displacement reaches half that square side. The four boundary crossings identify the full span; choose the earliest and latest along the common direction. Coincident centers admit a convenient vertical direction.
correctness: A line bisecting a square passes through its center, and central symmetry pairs equal areas on its two sides. When centers differ, the line through both bisects each; when equal, any nonzero direction does. For direction (dx,dy), a boundary is reached at parameter distance side/(2*max(abs(dx),abs(dy))) from that square center, because at least one axis reaches its half-side and neither exceeds it sooner. Computing both signed crossings for both squares gives the complete segment portions. Their smallest and largest direction parameters are exactly the outer endpoints across the two portions. Returning those endpoints therefore specifies a common area bisector and its full required span.
walkthrough: Squares [0,0,2] and [4,0,2] have centers [1,1] and [5,1]. Their common bisector is y=1 and the outer crossings are [0,1] and [6,1], so return [0,1,6,1]. For identical [0,0,2] squares, vertical [1,0,1,2] and horizontal [0,1,2,1] are both accepted.
time: O(1) center, direction and boundary calculations for exactly two squares.
space: O(1) auxiliary scalars and four returned coordinates.
edges: Horizontal/vertical/diagonal center lines and fractional crossings.
Disjoint, overlapping, nested, identical and concentric squares.
Different side lengths, negative positions and boundary coordinates.
related: The public square cut returns the outer segment through both centers. This binding states axis orientation, endpoint span and the nonunique concentric-center case without imposing an arbitrary orientation on valid solutions.
title: Bisect Squares

python.signature: def BisectSquares(squares: list[list[int]]) -> list[float]
python.starterCode:
def BisectSquares(squares: list[list[int]]) -> list[float]:
    return []
python.solutionCode:
def BisectSquares(squares: list[list[int]]) -> list[float]:
    x = squares[0][0] + squares[0][2] / 2.0
    y = squares[0][1] + squares[0][2] / 2.0
    dx = squares[1][0] + squares[1][2] / 2.0 - x
    dy = squares[1][1] + squares[1][2] / 2.0 - y
    if dx == 0 and dy == 0:
        dy = 1.0
        other = 0.0
    else:
        other = 1.0
    scale = max(abs(dx), abs(dy))
    first_radius = squares[0][2] / (2.0 * scale)
    second_radius = squares[1][2] / (2.0 * scale)
    start = min(-first_radius, other - second_radius)
    end = max(first_radius, other + second_radius)
    return [x + start * dx, y + start * dy, x + end * dx, y + end * dy]

description: Find a straight line passing through the largest number of input point occurrences. Return integer coefficients [A,B,C] for A*x+B*y+C=0, with A and B not both zero. Any maximum line is accepted, including equivalent coefficient scaling/sign. Collinearity is exact, with no floating-point epsilon.
constraints: points is a nonnull array of 0..100 nonnull [x,y] rows, with coordinates in -1000..1000. Duplicate coordinates are allowed and each original occurrence counts. Preserve the outer array, original rows, values and order.

Return three signed 32-bit coefficients for a nonempty input. Every nonempty integer-point set has a suitable maximum line with representable integer coefficients. Empty input returns []. For one point or all coincident points, any valid line through that location is accepted; the reference chooses a vertical line.
why: Fix one input point as an anchor. Every different point on one line through it has the same reduced direction after dividing by gcd and normalizing orientation. Count those direction groups and add coincident occurrences to every group. Repeat for every anchor, keeping the highest score. This stores only one anchor's groups rather than every pairwise line object.
correctness: For a fixed anchor, normalized directions agree exactly for points on the same undirected line through it; gcd reduction avoids fractional/vertical special guesses. Coincident occurrences lie on every such line and must be added to each group. For any maximum line containing distinct locations, its earliest original anchor has all its other occurrences among the later points, so that anchor's group reaches the full optimum count. No reported group can exceed the true optimum because its coefficients define a real line through all counted occurrences. All-coincident input is covered by the explicit vertical fallback. Integer cross-products give exact membership without tolerance ambiguity.
walkthrough: For [[0,0],[1,1],[2,2],[0,1]], anchoring at [0,0] groups [1,1] and [2,2] under reduced direction (1,1). That line has three occurrences and equation x-y=0, so [1,-1,0] is valid. Vertical lines use B=0; repeated [0,0] occurrences add to every line through that anchor.
time: Expected O(n^2*log(C+1)) arithmetic/hash work for coordinate-difference bound C=2000, hence expected O(n^2) in this fixed domain. Hash collisions can worsen the bound.
space: O(n) direction counts for one anchor plus constant-size returned coefficients.
edges: No points, one point and all coincident points.
Vertical/horizontal lines, negative slopes, duplicate occurrences and multiple optimal lines.
Nearly parallel rational slopes must remain distinct; exact integer arithmetic replaces an epsilon guess.
related: The author task asks for the line through most points. Bounded integer coordinates and integer line equations preserve that task while making vertical, duplicate and numerical-boundary behavior explicit.

description: Score a four-slot Master Mind guess against a secret. Both strings contain only R,G,B,Y. A hit is a matching color in the same slot. A pseudo-hit is a correct color in a different slot after hits have been removed. Each remaining secret occurrence may be used at most once. Return [hits,pseudoHits].
constraints: guess and secret are nonnull strings of exactly four uppercase ASCII characters from R,G,B,Y. Repeated colors are allowed. Preserve both inputs.
A hit cannot also be a pseudo-hit. Excess guessed occurrences of a color receive no credit beyond the unmatched secret count.
why: Reserve exact matches first so their occurrences cannot be reused. Among the unmatched positions, only remaining color multiplicities matter: each unmatched guess can consume one occurrence of its color if available. A frequency table implements this matching without pairing the same secret slot twice.
correctness: The first pass counts every exact match and excludes both its occurrences from later matching. For each other secret slot, it adds one available occurrence of that color. The second pass ignores hit slots and consumes an available matching color for each unmatched guess. For every color this creates exactly the minimum of its unmatched guess and secret multiplicities, which is the greatest possible one-to-one matching count. Colors are disjoint, so their sum is the pseudo-hit count.
walkthrough: For guess GGRR and secret RGBY, slot 1 is a G hit. Remaining secret colors are R,B,Y; remaining guesses are G,R,R. Only one R can consume the single remaining R, so the score is [1,1], not [1,2].
time: O(1) for the fixed four slots; two passes and a fixed four-color table.
space: O(1) auxiliary space and a two-integer result.
edges: All hits, no matches, all one color.
Repeated guessed colors cannot consume one unmatched secret occurrence twice.
related: The bank returns two integers rather than a language-specific Result class; scoring semantics are unchanged.

description: Return the inclusive zero-based endpoints [left,right] of the shortest contiguous window which, if sorted in nondecreasing order, would make the entire array nondecreasing. Do not actually change the input. If it is already sorted, including an empty or singleton array, return [-1,-1].
constraints: values contains 0..10000 signed 32-bit integers. Duplicates are allowed. Preserve the input array and order.
Equal adjacent values are already in sorted order. The returned endpoints describe the window in the original array.
why: Scanning left to right, any value below the largest earlier value is too far right and must lie inside the sorting window. Its last occurrence of such a violation fixes the right endpoint. Symmetrically, a value above the smallest later value is too far left; scanning backward locates the left endpoint. This avoids sorting a full copy just to find mismatches.
correctness: At each forward position, the running maximum equals the maximum of the prefix. A value smaller than that maximum cannot be fixed without including its position, so the last such position is a necessary right bound. The reverse argument makes the first position above its suffix minimum a necessary left bound. Outside those bounds, values are ordered consistently with all preceding or following values. Sorting the enclosed region therefore removes all cross-order violations and makes the whole array nondecreasing. Since neither bound can be excluded, the resulting window is shortest. No forward violation means no inversion and hence an already sorted array.
walkthrough: For [1,2,4,3,3,5], the running maximum becomes 4 at index 2; indices 3 and 4 are below it, so right=4. Scanning backward, the suffix minimum is 3 when index 2 is reached, giving left=2. Sorting indices 2..4 produces [1,2,3,3,4,5].
time: O(n) time for two scans.
space: O(1) auxiliary storage, excluding the two-integer output.
edges: Empty, singleton, already sorted, all equal.
Reverse order, duplicates around both endpoints, signed extremes.
related: The public source's already-sorted range is not a useful empty-window signal; [-1,-1] is explicit here.
title: Sub Sort

description: Return the largest sum of a contiguous sequence of values. The empty sequence is allowed and has sum zero, so an empty array or all-negative array returns zero. Preserve the input; return the sum rather than sequence endpoints.
constraints: values has 0..1000 integers, each in -1000000..1000000. Every contiguous sum is within signed 32-bit range. The input is nonnull and unchanged.

A sequence must use consecutive positions in their original order. Do not select separated positive values. Empty-sequence permission is intentional and matches the public source's zero result for all-negative input.
why: For any next element, a best suffix either extends a nonnegative previous suffix or starts afresh. A negative running prefix can never improve a future sum, so discard it. Retain a separate best-so-far total so ending a promising sequence does not lose its result.
correctness: After processing a prefix, running is the maximum of zero and the sums of all suffixes of that prefix. Appending the next value extends every nonempty candidate suffix; taking max(0,running+value) also permits the empty suffix and subsumes starting with this value alone. Induction preserves that invariant. Every contiguous sequence ends at some position, so updating best with every running value finds the greatest of all sequence sums, including the empty sequence.
walkthrough: For [2,-8,3,-2,4,-10], running totals after discarding negative suffixes are 2,0,3,1,5,0. The best is 5 from [3,-2,4]. Adding all positive elements would incorrectly return 9 because those positions are not contiguous.
time: O(n) time in one scan.
space: O(1) auxiliary scalar storage.
edges: Empty and all-negative inputs return zero.
Zeros, all-positive input, a best interval strictly inside the array.
related: A maximum-subarray variant requiring a nonempty sequence has different all-negative behavior and is not silently substituted.
title: Contiguous Sequence

python.signature: def MaximumContiguousSum(values: list[int]) -> int
python.starterCode:
def MaximumContiguousSum(values: list[int]) -> int:
    return 0
python.solutionCode:
def MaximumContiguousSum(values: list[int]) -> int:
    running = 0
    best = 0
    for value in values:
        running = max(0, running + value)
        best = max(best, running)
    return best

description: Determine whether replacing every a in pattern with one fixed string and every b with another fixed string can produce text exactly. Each replacement may be empty, and the two replacement strings may be equal. Every occurrence of the same symbol must use the same replacement.
constraints: pattern contains 0..20 symbols, each a or b. text contains 0..100 lowercase ASCII letters. Strings are nonnull and unchanged. This is concatenation substitution, not regular-expression matching.

An empty pattern matches only empty text. A nonempty pattern matches empty text by assigning empty replacements to its used symbols. An unused symbol imposes no constraint. Consume the whole text; matching a prefix is insufficient.
why: If a appears ca times and b appears cb times, candidate replacement lengths must satisfy ca*la+cb*lb=text.length. Enumerate one used length, derive the other, and verify every occurrence against the first substring assigned to its symbol. This avoids enumerating all possible replacement strings independently.
correctness: Every valid substitution has nonnegative lengths satisfying the total-length equation, so its length pair is among those tested. For a tested pair, scan pattern from left to right and assign a symbol the text slice at its first occurrence; later occurrences must equal that slice. This enforces consistent replacements and advances by exactly the chosen length. The total-length equation ensures the final offset is the text end. Thus any accepted pair defines a valid full substitution, and the pair of any valid substitution passes verification. Empty/unused-symbol cases follow the explicit zero-length and full-consumption rules.
walkthrough: For pattern=abba and text=redbluebluered, lengths a=3 and b=4 assign red at the first a and blue at the first b. The second b matches blue and the last a matches red, consuming all text, so return true. For pattern=ab and text=x, a may be empty and b=x; distinct nonempty replacements are not required.
time: O((n+1)*(n+p+1)) conservative time for text length n and pattern length p: at most n+1 length choices, with O(n+p) slice/comparison work each.
space: O(n) replacement-slice storage plus O(1) counters; no expanded candidate string is built.
edges: Empty pattern/text and a pattern using only one symbol.
Empty or equal replacement strings, mismatched repeated symbols and unmatched trailing text.
related: The public exhaustive construction allows empty and equal substitutions. The bank states those rules explicitly and checks exact total length, including the one-symbol case.

description: Find every pond in a rectangular elevation grid and return its size in cells, sorted in increasing order. Elevation 0 is water; positive elevations are land. Water cells belong to one pond when connected horizontally, vertically or diagonally, through any number of water cells. Keep one size per pond, including repeated equal sizes.
constraints: land is nonnull with 0..50 rows and 0..50 columns, rectangular rows, and integer elevations 0..10000. Empty dimensions or a grid without water return an empty collection.

Preserve the outer array, original rows and every elevation. Use a separate visited structure instead of overwriting water or land. Eight-neighbor connectivity is intentional and differs from four-neighbor paint fill. Return a materialized integer array/list/vector in increasing order.
why: Start a search only at an unvisited water cell, mark it on discovery, and count every water cell reached through eight-neighbor steps. Every such search consumes exactly one connected component. Separate visited flags preserve the elevation input; marking before pushing avoids counting a water cell twice. Sorting the component counts provides the bank's deterministic output order without merging equal-sized ponds.
correctness: The search starts within one pond, and each discovered water neighbor is connected to a reached water cell, so it remains in that same pond. Every water cell in the pond has a water path from the start; induction along that path shows it is eventually reached. Marking at discovery gives exactly one count per cell. The outer scan starts no later search in an already visited component, while every other pond eventually supplies an unvisited starting cell. Thus the recorded sizes include every pond once. Sorting changes only their order, not multiplicity, and the elevation grid is never changed.
walkthrough: In [[0,1,0],[1,0,1],[0,1,0]], the center water cell touches every corner diagonally. All five zeros are therefore one pond, so return [5]. Four-neighbor searches would incorrectly report five ponds of size one.
time: O(rows*columns + p*log(p+1)) time for the scan/search and sorting p pond sizes. Each cell and its eight neighbors are checked a constant number of times.
space: O(rows*columns) visited flags and worst-case work stack, excluding the p returned sizes.
edges: No water, all water, empty dimensions.
Diagonal-only connections, separate equal-sized ponds, and boundary/corner cells.
related: Increasing size order is a bank convention; preserving inputs follows the author's separate-visited variant rather than its mutating alternative.

description: Find one value from each array that could be exchanged to make the array sums equal. Return [valueFromFirst,valueFromSecond], or [] if no such exchange exists. Do not actually exchange or modify entries. If several exchanges work, choose the value at the earliest original position in first; its matching second value is then determined.
constraints: Each input is a nonnull array of 0..1000 signed 32-bit integers. Values may repeat. Both chosen values must actually occur in their respective arrays. An empty array cannot supply an exchange, even when both sums are equal.

Preserve both arrays and their order. Compute sums and candidate differences in signed 64-bit arithmetic (or Python int / exact JavaScript Number); the admitted maximum absolute total difference is below 2^53. A candidate outside signed 32-bit range is not an array value and must not be narrowed with wraparound.
why: Writing the new sums as S1-a+b and S2-b+a gives 2*(a-b)=S1-S2. An odd total difference is impossible. Otherwise, for each a in first, the only possible b is a-(S1-S2)/2; a hash set of second values answers membership without testing every pair.
correctness: Any valid exchange satisfies the derived equation, so an odd sum difference rules out all possibilities. For an even difference, every scanned a has exactly one required b. A set membership hit proves both values occur and substitution into the equation proves the new sums agree. Conversely, every valid exchange has a first-array occurrence that the scan visits and its required second value is in the set, so a valid exchange cannot be missed. Scanning original first order and returning the first hit implements the tie rule. No hit proves absence.
walkthrough: For first=[4,1,2,1,1,2] (sum 11) and second=[3,6,3,3] (sum 15), the half-difference is -2. The first value 4 requires second value 6, which exists, so return [4,6]. The hypothetical new sums are both 13; the supplied arrays stay unchanged.
time: Expected O(n+m) time for sums, building the membership set and one scan; hash collisions can worsen the bound.
space: O(m) membership storage plus a constant-size returned pair.
edges: Empty inputs, odd total difference, equal sums but no shared value.

description: Simulate Langton's ant on an infinite initially white grid. The ant starts at row 0, column 0, facing right. On each step, turn right on white or left on black, flip the current cell, then move forward one cell. Return the final board as ASCII rows over the smallest rectangle containing every position the ant has visited, including its initial and final positions.
constraints: 0 <= steps <= 2000. Rows increase downward and columns increase rightward. Turning right is clockwise in this coordinate system. A newly entered cell is not inspected/flipped until the next step.

Render rows from smallest to largest row, and columns from smallest to largest column. Use . for white and # for black, except render the ant at its final position with R, D, L or U for its direction, hiding the cell color beneath it. Each returned string is one row, with no newline or footer.
The rectangle includes visited white cells even if all their black marks were later erased. For zero steps return ["R"]. Do not assume a fixed-size board or clip the walk.
why: Only visited cells can become black, so a sparse set records black coordinates while unlisted positions remain white. Track the extrema of every ant position separately: black-cell extrema alone can shrink incorrectly after flips. Once simulation ends, render that visited rectangle and overlay the final ant marker.
correctness: Initially the sparse set is empty and the ant state matches the all-white start. At each step, membership gives the exact current color by induction. The corresponding turn, membership toggle and one-cell movement implement the three required actions in order, preserving the exact state invariant. Updating coordinate extrema after every movement, from the initial zero bounds, records all visited positions including the final destination. Rendering each bounded coordinate therefore produces the required rectangle, cell colors and final orientation marker without losing erased white positions.
walkthrough: At zero steps the board is [R]. Step 1 sees white, turns from right to down, colors (0,0) black and moves to (1,0), yielding ["#","D"]. Step 2 turns from down to left on white, flips (1,0), and moves to (1,-1). The visited rectangle now has two columns, yielding [".#","L#"].
time: Expected O(steps+A) time for sparse-set simulation and rendering A cells of the visited bounding rectangle; A is O((steps+1)^2) in the worst case.
space: O(steps+A) storage for black coordinates and returned board characters. The simulation does not allocate an infinite or full worst-case grid.
edges: Zero steps and the first turns before a black cell is revisited.
A black-cell left turn, erased marks, negative coordinates and the 2000-step boundary.
related: The author sparse Board tracks all visited extrema and starts facing right. ASCII markers and returned rows replace its Unicode arrows/newline/footer presentation.
title: Langtons Ant

python.solutionCode:
def LangtonBoard(steps: int) -> list[str]:
    black = set()
    row = column = direction = 0
    min_row = max_row = min_column = max_column = 0
    dr, dc = [0, 1, 0, -1], [1, 0, -1, 0]
    for _ in range(steps):
        position = (row, column)
        if position in black:
            direction = (direction + 3) % 4
            black.remove(position)
        else:
            direction = (direction + 1) % 4
            black.add(position)
        row += dr[direction]
        column += dc[direction]
        min_row, max_row = min(min_row, row), max(max_row, row)
        min_column, max_column = min(min_column, column), max(max_column, column)
    result = []
    for r in range(min_row, max_row + 1):
        line = []
        for c in range(min_column, max_column + 1):
            line.append(
                "RDLU"[direction] if (r, c) == (row, column) else "#" if (r, c) in black else "."
            )
        result.append("".join(line))
    return result

description: Form as many disjoint pairs of input occurrences as possible whose values sum to target. Each occurrence may be used in at most one pair. Return each pair as [smallerValue,largerValue], and return the pairs in lexicographic order. Repeated equal pairs are retained when enough occurrences exist; this is not a list of every index pair.
constraints: values is a nonnull array of 0..1000 signed 32-bit integers; target is signed 32-bit. Preserve values and its order. Return a concrete two-dimensional integer collection, with exactly two values per row.

A pair uses two distinct occurrences, including when the values are equal. Use widened arithmetic for pair sums so signed endpoints do not wrap. Empty or singleton input returns []. Ordering is a deterministic presentation convention; occurrence consumption follows the author sorted two-pointer variant.
why: Sort a private copy and inspect its smallest and largest remaining values. If their sum is too small, the smallest cannot pair with anything; if too large, the largest cannot pair with anything. On equality, consume both occurrences. Complementary value classes cannot compete with other classes, so using a valid pair cannot reduce the eventual pair count.
correctness: For sorted endpoints a<=b, a+b<target means no remaining partner is large enough for a; discarding a loses no valid pair. Similarly a+b>target rules out every remaining partner for b. On equality, a can pair only with value b and b only with value a. Taking that pair reduces the available counts of those complementary classes by one each (or by two for equal values), achieving the maximum possible count for that class. Repeating these safe steps produces a maximum number of disjoint pairs. Left endpoints never decrease, so normalized pairs are already in lexicographic order; all are drawn from distinct consumed occurrences.
walkthrough: For values=[1,1,2,2,3,3] and target 4, the sorted endpoints yield [1,3], then another [1,3], then [2,2]. All six occurrences are used once. With only three 2s and target 4, return one [2,2], leaving one unused; returning three index pairs would reuse occurrences.
time: O(n log(n+1)) time for sorting plus O(n) endpoint steps.
space: O(n) for the private sorted copy and O(p) returned pairs, p<=floor(n/2).
edges: No pair, singleton, duplicate pairs and odd equal-value multiplicity.
Negative targets, zero and signed endpoints requiring widened sums.
related: The public hash-count and sorted variants consume occurrences, while its brute-force variant enumerates index pairs. This callable explicitly selects the disjoint sorted variant rather than hiding that distinction.

description: Implement a fixed-capacity least-recently-used cache with integer keys and string values. Get(key) returns the stored string and marks an existing entry most recently used; an absent key returns null and does not change recency. Set(key,value) inserts or replaces an entry and marks it most recently used. Inserting a new key into a full cache evicts the least recently used entry.
constraints: capacity is 1..1000. The operation transcript has 1..2001 entries and starts with LRUCache; remaining entries are Get or Set. keys and values have the same length as operations. Constructor placeholders are key=0,value=""; Get has an unused value="". Set uses both its key and string value.

Keys are signed 32-bit integers. Set values are nonnull strings of 0..20 printable ASCII characters, including the empty string. A missing Get returns null, which differs from a stored empty string. Constructor and Set return no value, represented by null. Return one output per operation in order.

Construct a fresh cache for each transcript; capacity and data must not leak between instances. Preserve transcript arrays and strings. Replacing an existing key does not consume another slot. Aim for expected constant-time lookup, refresh and eviction rather than scanning all entries.
why: Lookup needs a key index, while eviction needs a recency order that supports removing an arbitrary accessed entry and adding it at the most-recent end. A dictionary plus doubly linked list provides both. Languages with an ordered-map facility can use its equivalent movement operations; an ordinary successful lookup alone does not necessarily refresh recency.
correctness: Maintain exactly one indexed entry for each cached key and an order from least to most recently used. A missing Get changes neither structure. An existing Get or Set moves its one entry to the most-recent end; Set also stores the new value. A new Set appends one entry and, only when capacity is exceeded, removes the oldest entry from both index and order. These updates preserve one-to-one membership, correct values and recency after every operation. Thus each eviction selects precisely the least recently used surviving key, and every Get returns the current value or null exactly when absent.
walkthrough: With capacity 2, Set(1,A), Set(2,B) orders keys [1,2]. Get(1) returns A and changes order to [2,1]. Set(3,C) evicts 2, leaving [1,3]. Get(2) returns null without refreshing anything; Get(1) still returns A. With capacity 1, Set(7,"") followed by Get(7) returns an empty string, not null.
time: Expected O(1) per Get/Set under conventional hash/ordered-map implementations; hash collisions can worsen access. JavaScript Map specifies average sublinear access rather than a strict constant-time guarantee. Value copying costs O(value.length) where applicable.
space: O(capacity) entries plus stored key/value data; the returned transcript uses O(operationCount) slots. Values are at most 20 characters.
edges: Capacity one, absent Get, repeated Set of an existing key and successful Get recency refresh.
Empty stored strings versus missing null; signed-endpoint keys.
Repeated evictions and fresh instances with independent capacities and state.
related: The author public cache uses integer keys and string values. Get/Set retain those payload types; a flat, explicitly aligned transcript makes constructor and operation results executable without a mixed-type argument matrix.

languageWhy.csharp: C# indexes LinkedListNode<(int Key,string Text)> objects in a Dictionary. Removing and re-adding the same node at the list tail refreshes recency without a linear key search. Replacing a value updates that node rather than creating a duplicate entry.
languageWhy.java: Java LinkedHashMap is constructed with accessOrder=true. Its successful get and put refresh order; after a new insertion exceeds capacity, the first key iterator entry is the least recently used and is removed. Default insertion-order LinkedHashMap would not implement Get refresh.
languageWhy.python: Python OrderedDict keeps the recency order. Assignment alone does not move an existing key, so Set explicitly calls move_to_end, as does successful Get. popitem(last=False) removes the least-recent entry. Missing None differs from a stored empty string.
languageWhy.javascript: JavaScript Map preserves insertion order, but get does not move a key. Successful Get deletes and reinserts the same key/value, and Set also deletes before insertion. The first keys() iterator entry is therefore the eviction candidate; missing Get returns null explicitly.
languageWhy.cpp: C++ indexes std::list iterators in an unordered_map. list::splice moves an accessed node to the tail in constant time while preserving its iterator, avoiding rescanning or rebuilding the index. std::optional<string> distinguishes absence from a stored empty string.

description: Evaluate an arithmetic expression containing nonnegative decimal integer literals and the binary operators +, -, * and /. Multiplication and division take precedence over addition and subtraction; operators of equal precedence associate left to right. Division is real division, not integer truncation. Return the finite numeric result.
constraints: expression has grammar integer (operator integer)*, with 1..51 literals, each 0..100. An integer is 0 or a digit 1..9 followed by digits; leading zeros, whitespace, parentheses, unary signs and decimal literals are outside this input domain. Every divisor literal is positive.

Every multiplication/division chain intermediate and every left-to-right addition/subtraction subtotal has absolute value at most 1000000. Return a number within max(0.000001, 0.000000001*abs(exactResult)) of the mathematical result. Preserve the input string.
why: Addition and subtraction separate an expression into signed multiplication/division chains. Keep the current chain in term and the sum of completed chains in total. A high-precedence operator extends term; a + or - commits the completed term and begins a new signed term. This preserves precedence without a stack or eval.
correctness: After each parsed literal, total is the sum of all completed additive chains and term is the value of the current chain, with its leading additive sign. Multiplication or division applies to term immediately, preserving left associativity. At an additive boundary, the chain is complete, so transferring it to total cannot be affected by later high-precedence operations. Starting the next literal with its additive sign maintains the invariant. At end, total+term includes every chain exactly once and equals the required expression value. The stated magnitude bounds control floating-point error; division by zero is excluded.
walkthrough: For 8/4/2+3*5-6, term becomes 8, then 2, then 1: division is left associative. The + commits 1 and starts 3; * extends it to 15. The - commits 15 and starts -6. The result is 1+15-6=10. For 1/2, the result is 0.5, not 0.
time: O(L) time for L expression characters; each digit/operator is read once.
space: O(1) auxiliary scalar state beyond the immutable input and scalar result.
edges: One literal, zero numerators and fractional division.
Mixed precedence, consecutive divisions and subtraction before a multiplication/division chain.
Maximum literals and bounded intermediate values; invalid syntax and zero divisors are outside the admitted expression domain.
related: The public calculator returns double and parses binary arithmetic on integer literals without parentheses. This independent binding states grammar, real division, associativity and numeric tolerance explicitly.
